title: Diffusion models for the $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model
abstract: A score-based diffusion model is trained on the two-dimensional classical Heisenberg model, the lattice representation of the $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model. Neural networks are trained on three different coarse-grainings of the same training set to implement a multiscale sampling scheme that modestly improves both the accuracy and computational cost of direct sampling on the finest lattice. Stein (or Schwinger-Dyson) diagnostics for the two-point correlation function are introduced to assess the quality of the learned score without relying on reverse diffusion sampling. These diagnostics are also incorporated into an additional training loss. We discuss several technical considerations relevant to implementing diffusion models on $S^2$. These include a consideration of lifting the network input to $S^3$, as in the $CP^1$ representation, and developing a boundary-layer approximation to the short-time spherical heat kernel that extends its usefulness to larger diffusion times.
summary: This work applies score-based diffusion models to simulate the 2D $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model, a challenging system in statistical mechanics. By training these generative models on coarse-grained lattice data, the authors develop a powerful, scalable alternative to traditional MCMC sampling. The results demonstrate that diffusion models can accurately predict key physical properties, such as correlation functions and topological susceptibility, thereby advancing the field of ML-enhanced computational physics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently sampling configurations for the $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model, which is computationally difficult using conventional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods.
main_result: The authors successfully apply score-based diffusion models to generate configurations for the model, showing that these methods can accurately reproduce key physical observables like correlation functions and topological susceptibility.
method: They train diffusion models on coarse-grained data from the lattice model, incorporating specialized diagnostics (Stein/Schwinger-Dyson) and handling the geometry of the $S^2$ manifold.
model_or_system: The system is the two-dimensional $O(3)$ nonlinear sigma model (classical Heisenberg model) on a lattice, which is studied in its continuum limit and on discrete lattices.
key_observables: Two-point correlation function, magnetic susceptibility ($\chi_m$), and topological susceptibility ($\chi_t$).
important_parameters: The coupling constant $ eta$ (set to 1.5), lattice size ($64^2, 32^2, 16^2$), and correlation length scales.
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions involve the applicability of diffusion models to lattice field theories and the development of approximations for the heat kernel on $S^2$.
figures_summary: Figures compare observables like $C(1)$, $C(32)$, $\chi_m$, and $\chi_t$ generated by diffusion models (DM16) against reference heat-bath simulations, demonstrating convergence.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical model and the limitations of MCMC, details the diffusion model framework (training, multiscale approach), presents the specialized diagnostics for manifold geometry, and concludes with comparisons of key thermodynamic observables.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the methodology—using advanced generative ML models to overcome sampling bottlenecks in complex physical systems—is highly relevant to developing efficient simulation techniques for quantum many-body systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A two-point correlation function for an O(3) model coarse-grained from a 642 lattice (β = 1.5) to a 162 lattice (black). One-parameter renormalizations of β to β′, fitting either the correlation length (blue) or the energy per site (red), are compared to the generated configurations from a diffusion model (purple). See also Table 1.

Figure 2: Distributions of the topological charge Q (left) and the number of lattice dislocations Ndis (right) for the two-dimensional O(3) model at β = 1.5 on a 642 lattice. The equilibrium heat-bath reference (black line) is compared with 104 configurations generated by a diffusion model using 800 score evaluations (blue histogram). Systematic errors in the configurations generated by the model are largely corrected after a cheap refinement of four heat-bath sweeps (purple error bars).

Figure 3: Editing short-distance structure with diffusion models. Configurations of classical spins are visualized by mapping spin orientations to saturated colors. An image of Seurat’s painting A Sunday Af- ternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte is first converted to saturated colors and then to a corresponding spin configuration. A diffusion model trained on the O(3) model at β = 1.5 is then used to modify the short-distance structure in a manner consistent with the local statistics of the equilibrium field theory. Figure 4: Comparison of approximations to the scalar score ∂z log K(θ, τ), where z = cos θ. The spectral expansion with ℓmax = 10 is used at large τ, while the MPSD and boundary-layer approximations are used at small τ. These approximations are shown at the switching time τ = 0.137, alongside a higher-order spectral expansion (ℓmax = 15).

Figure 5: Two-point correlation function C(r) on the 642 lattice. Solid lines show equilibrium correlations at diffusion times u = 0, 0.5, and 0.75, while circles show the corresponding Stein estimates (40). Diamonds show correlations measured from configurations generated by the diffusion model using 800 score evaluations.
